title: Fashion Design Basics
summary: Start your journey in fashion: the fashion world and African textiles, elements and principles of design, fabrics and estimating yardage, measurements, ease and pattern making, garment construction and quality, and costing, pricing and running a fashion business. Calculations were checked in code.
audience: Aspiring designers, tailors, dressmakers and fashion entrepreneurs

body.p: Fashion design creates clothing and accessories that combine function, beauty and identity. Designers research trends and culture, sketch ideas, choose fabrics, develop patterns and samples, and work with makers to produce garments that people want to wear.

Africa has a rich textile heritage: kente from Ghana, bogolan (mud cloth) from Mali, adire from Nigeria, kanga and kitenge from East Africa, shweshwe from South Africa and many more. African designers now show at fashion weeks in Lagos, Johannesburg, Accra, Nairobi and Dakar, and globally. When using traditional textiles and symbols, respect their meanings and the communities that created them, and credit and pay artisans fairly.

list: Haute couture and bespoke: made-to-measure, handcrafted, expensive.
Ready-to-wear and designer labels: produced in standard sizes in smaller runs.
Mass market: high volumes at lower prices.
Custom tailoring for clients, a large part of African fashion businesses.

body.tip: Keep a sketchbook and photograph details you love: colours, prints, street style and architecture all inspire design.

list: Line: seams, darts, hems and prints create lines that lead the eye; vertical lines can lengthen a figure.
Shape and silhouette: the outline of a garment, such as A-line, fitted, oversized or empire line.
Colour: hue, value and intensity create mood; consider colour combinations and how colours suit different skin tones.
Texture: how fabric looks and feels, from smooth silk to rough linen.
Pattern: prints and weaves, from wax prints to stripes.
Balance: symmetrical or asymmetrical.
Proportion: the relationship of parts, such as bodice to skirt length.
Emphasis: a focal point, such as a bold sleeve or neckline.
Rhythm: repeated elements such as pleats or buttons.
Harmony: all parts working together.

body.p: Designers use these tools to solve problems: making a garment comfortable in heat, flattering for different body shapes, and suitable for the occasion.

body.tip: When a design feels wrong, check proportion first; small changes in length often fix it.

list: Natural fibres: cotton (breathable, ideal for warm climates), linen (cool and crisp), silk (smooth and luxurious) and wool (warm).
Synthetic fibres: polyester and nylon are durable and cheap but less breathable; blends combine properties.
Regenerated fibres such as viscose drape well.

body.p: Woven fabrics (such as poplin, denim and wax print) are stable; knitted fabrics (such as jersey) stretch. Grain matters: cutting on the straight grain keeps garments hanging correctly, while cutting on the bias (at 45°) gives drape and stretch. Pre-wash fabrics that may shrink, especially cotton, before cutting.
If one dress needs 1.5 m of fabric, four dresses need 4 x 1.5 = 6 m. Add about 15% for matching prints, shrinkage and mistakes: 6 x 1.15 = about 6.9 m.

body.tip: Ask for fabric swatches and test them: wash, iron and stretch them before buying in bulk.

body.p: Accurate measurements are the foundation of a good fit. Measure over light clothing with a flexible tape held snug but not tight.

list: Key measurements: bust or chest, waist, hips, shoulder width, back length, arm length, inseam and garment length.
Ease is extra room added for movement and style. A bodice for a 92 cm bust with 6 cm of ease is drafted for 98 cm; a quarter-front pattern piece then uses 98 / 4 = 24.5 cm.
Record measurements on a client card with the date.

body.p: A pattern is a template for cutting fabric. Designers start from a basic block (sloper) of the body shape and adapt it with darts, pleats, gathers and style lines. Patterns can be drafted by hand, draped on a dress form, or made digitally with pattern software. Mark grain lines, notches, seam allowances (commonly 1 to 1.5 cm) and cutting instructions on every piece.
Grading creates the same pattern in different sizes, essential for ready-to-wear.

body.tip: Make a test garment (a toile or muslin) in cheap fabric before cutting expensive material.

steps: Lay out pattern pieces on the grain, pin or weight them, and cut accurately.
Transfer markings such as darts and notches.
Sew darts and main seams, pressing each seam as you go.
Attach collars, sleeves, waistbands and closures such as zips and buttons.
Finish seams to prevent fraying, with overlocking, zigzag or bound seams.
Hem, give a final press and check quality.

list: Even stitching and straight seams.
Matching prints at seams where possible.
Secure buttons and smooth zips.
No loose threads, and a correct fit on the client or dress form.

body.p: An industrial straight-stitch machine and an overlocker are the core equipment of a small workshop.

body.tip: Press as you sew: pressing each seam before crossing it gives a professional finish.

body.p: Calculate the full cost of each garment: materials R150, labour R100 and a share of overheads such as rent and electricity R50 give a cost of R300. With a 50% markup the price is R450, a profit margin of about 33%. Selling 20 garments gives revenue of R9000 and a gross profit of R3000.

list: Build a portfolio and photograph work well, in good light on real people.
Sell through social media, markets, pop-up shops and online stores.
Take deposits on custom orders and agree delivery dates in writing.
Protect your brand name and logo; consider trademark registration.
Consider sustainability: reduce fabric waste, use offcuts, offer repairs and source responsibly.

body.p: Fashion careers include designer, pattern maker, tailor, stylist, textile designer, buyer, merchandiser and fashion photographer.

body.tip: Never underprice to win customers; price for your skill, time and costs, or the business will not survive.
